app/Sources/AiTermUI

AiTerm Design System

Swift is the source of truth. The system is the code in app/Sources/AiTermUI/ and the rules in its README.md. There is no generated token file, no canvas and no build step.

This page is a human view of that code, synced on request by the design-system skill. When the two disagree, the Swift wins — and you never need this page to write correct Swift.

  1. Reuse before new. A new variant or content case on an existing primitive. Badge absorbed three bespoke types this way.
  2. A pattern — existing primitives arranged. It keeps an AiTerm name and lives in Views/, not in the library.
  3. A genuinely new primitive. It owes a standard name, every measurement from Metrics, every colour from Palette, a declared variant × state matrix, a line in the README's inventory, and a test under app/Tests/AiTermUITests/.
Palette.swift
Every colour. A literal graphite ramp of grounds, inks and hairlines, the AppKit accent and status colours, brand marks, and the washes.
Metrics.swift
Space, Radius, Size, Typography, Sheet, Opacity, Motion — every height, radius, spacing and text size, the one fade for a disabled control, and the one ease-out.
Surface.swift
The ground a component is drawn on, read from the environment.
ControlChrome.swift
focusRing, fieldChrome, chipChrome, fieldBox, menuChrome, menuRowHighlight, groupChrome — the house chrome.
RingGeometry.swift
The round marks' shared stroke, 15 % of their diameter, and the half-stroke inset that keeps a trimmed or centred stroke inside it.
InterfaceScale.swift
How much larger than Apple's sizes the sidebar is drawn, read from the environment like Surface.
IconSource.swift
Logos.swift
One way to name any mark the app draws, and the vendor paths it draws them from. Logos and LogoGlyph are internal to the module.
README.md
The rules: two tiers, reuse before new, one theme, states are a matrix.
AiTerm/Views/
The patterns. AiTerm names, AiTerm concepts, primitives only.

Colour

AiTerm is dark-only, so its greys are literal values rather than AppKit's semantic colours: a graphite ramp of grounds, three inks and two hairlines. Grounds rise from the well to the lightest control ground, and a field is drawn a step darker than what holds it while a button is a step lighter. Grounds are the same with or without Increase Contrast; the inks and hairlines resolve to a stronger value of their own under it, so a view needs to know nothing about the setting. The accent, the status colours and the link stay AppKit's; brand marks keep their vendor colours. A colour derived from another, a wash, a dimmed ink, a pressed state, is a named member too, never an .opacity(…) written in a view.

One more rule, enforced by PaletteDistinctionTests: every distinctly-written token must resolve to a distinct colour, in the dark appearance or under Increase Contrast. Where two roles share a value it is declared as an alias in the source, and shown as one here. The test exists because a hover wash once resolved to the surface it was painted over and drew a visible halo around every hovered avatar.

The greys are definitions; the accent family is resolved. Every ground, ink and hairline below is the literal the Swift writes. The accent, the status colours, the link and the placeholder are AppKit's own, read back under .darkAqua; the accent and everything derived from it follow the accent chosen in System Settings and are shown at the default blue. Where an ink or a hairline has an Increase Contrast value, it is given after IC.

Brand marks

A Brand derives its Color, its hex string, its SVG path and its fallback SF Symbol from one number, which is what stops the two forms drifting — #2684FF used to be written once as Palette.jira and once as a literal inside the old Jira chip. These are vendor colours, not UI colours: never reach for one to colour a button or a status.

Surface

A component reads the ground it sits on from the environment, @Environment(\.surface), set with .surface(_:), instead of taking a selected: Bool. Each case publishes its own ink, secondary ink, badge wash, hovered badge wash and occluding background, so a badge inside a newly selected row strengthens its wash by itself rather than every call site re-deriving the same colours. Selection is neutral: a selected row lifts its title to white and keeps every mark's colour, amber, green, the spinner, the done ring, a brand. Only .accent, a primary button's label, turns everything on it white. Surface is not a component and gets no card; it is a rule the components assume.

A ring or divider painted over content needs occludingBackground rather than the wash: AvatarGroupView's ring has to hide the avatar behind it, and a translucent colour lets the stacked marks show through. .washed and .washedHover are the Operator's row, at rest and hovered: the sidebar plus Palette.operatorRow, or badgeHovered in its place. .selected is a selected sidebar row; .selectedOnSheet is a selected row on a sheet, the Archive's, inked the same and differing only in the ground beneath. .accent is for the primary button only. .sheet is the default.

Scale

Every number on this page is a size at ×1. It becomes points where a view reads it, at the environment's InterfaceScale — @Environment(\.interfaceScale), set with .interfaceScale(_:), like Surface. Typography scales by itself, because View.font(TypeStyle) reads the environment, and is not rounded, so text never outgrows the layout around it. Space, Radius and Size are read through scale(…) and land on whole points; at ×1 that is the identity. Strokes — hairlines, borders, rings, the focus ring — do not scale. A size: parameter is points on screen: the caller scales the token it passes, and a view scales only its own token reads.

Only the sidebar is scaled; SidebarSheet resets to .standard, so a sheet keeps Apple's sizes. Of the primitives, Badge and PushButtonStyle scale their own height, radius and padding (the empty sidebar's Add Project… is a .push(.secondary) like any sheet's), SidebarHeading and HelpText (under the empty sidebar's line) scale through their one token, a Typography style, and Hairline is a stroke; the rest are only drawn in sheets and read their tokens at ×1, and a primitive that moves into the sidebar must first read its tokens through scale. Select stays unscaled: its menu is a native NSPopUpButton. The person picks the step as InterfaceSize — Settings › Interface › Sidebar size, or View › Zoom In / Zoom Out / Actual Size — and the app maps it onto InterfaceScale.

Space

Space is the one house scale in the system — a 4-point rhythm, plus three named steps that earn their place inside chips, control tracks and field interiors, where the rhythm's own steps are the wrong size. Those three are marked below. Drawn at actual size.

hairline 2 pt ·
Inside a segmented track, between it and its selected segment.
tight 4 pt
Icon to label inside a chip.
snug 6 pt ·
A label to its control; a branch name to its +n chip.
base 8 pt
Related controls; a row's leading padding.
inset 10 pt ·
A text field's horizontal interior padding, and the gap from a row's avatar, or a footer row's vendor mark, to its text. Also the sidebar List's own inset, which the sidebar footer, below the list, adds back to line up with the rows. At 8 the text crowds the field's stroke; at 12 a short value looks lost.
gap 12 pt
Two fields side by side; the quiet badges along a sidebar row's subtitle line, which have no box to separate them.
block 16 pt
Field to field, section to section, and a sheet footer's padding.
section 20 pt
A task row's indent under its project; a sheet header's top.
margin 24 pt
The sheet gutter.

· off the 4-point rhythm, on purpose.

Radius

The house radii, a step rounder than AppKit's own (4, 6, 8 and a popover's 10): the layered foundation picked on 13 Nov 2026 draws every shape one step softer. Drawn at actual size.

Size

Heights, widths and diameters: the sidebar's own widths, every control and row height, and the marks drawn inside them. A field, a pop-up button, a segmented track and a push button are all 28 pt because that is what .controlSize(.large) measures, not because 28 looked balanced. Drawn at actual size.

tabIndicator 2 pt
The bar under a TabBar's selected tab, drawn over the sheet header's rule: twice a hairline, so it reads as the selection rather than as a second rule. A stroke, so it does not scale.
statusMarkSmall 8 pt
The status mark inside a count chip, where the usual size would overflow it; and a ToneRing, leading a Settings card's status line and the footer's Backpack Mode line.
statusMark 10 pt
A status mark on a row, and the sidebar footer's rings drawn to its recipe. A row's mark sits in the trailing column, so this is declared as an alias: statusMark = trailingGlyph.
trailingGlyph 10 pt
The ink in the sidebar's trailing column, centred in a slot.
chevron 10 pt
The column a project row's disclosure chevron sits in, leading its provider mark. Its own name, not trailingGlyph's: that one feeds the trailing column's inset arithmetic, and a change there must not move this glyph.
pickerRowLogo 11 pt
A vendor mark in a picker's result row — smaller than pickerLogo, to sit inside a menuRow.
inlineMark 12 pt
A mark that leads a line of text and stands no taller than it: the Notice's amber exclamation mark beside its Typography.label title, and a background job's glyph in the background-work card.
pickerLogo 13 pt
A vendor mark beside a picked item in a picker's field: the ticket, the merge request, the Jira project.
chip 16 pt
Every chip: the Jira key, the VS Code badge, +n, a status count.
vendorMark 16 pt
A vendor mark outside an avatar group: the sidebar footer, the agent picker. A diameter that happens to equal chip's height.
avatar 18 pt
A vendor mark in an avatar group, and the provider tile beside a project name. Also an icon-only Badge's width.
slot 20 pt
The click target the sidebar's trailing column is built from.
menuRow 24 pt
A row in a menu, a dropdown or the completion popup; the sidebar's Projects header and a DividerRow; a sidebar footer row and its System and Usage headings. Also a Select's chevron slot.
control 28 pt
A field, a pop-up button (.controlSize(.large)), a segmented track, a push button (PushButtonStyle).
projectRow 28 pt
A project header. Same number as control, kept a separate name because it answers to a different scale.
pickerRequestKey 44 pt
A request's sigil and four-digit number in the picker results: PickerResultRow's key column in New Review's merge request picker.
row 52 pt
A task or terminal row: a 16 pt title, Space.tight, a 16 pt chip line, inside Space.base above and below. Was 44, which left 5 pt around the text.
pickerProjectKey 64 pt
A Jira project key without the ticket number, shared by both project pickers — ProjectSheet's and SignalSheet's: PickerResultRow's key column.
pickerTicketKey 74 pt
A ticket key of up to eight characters in the pickers' key face (Typography.caption, tabular): PickerResultRow's key column in TicketPickerField.
sidebarMinWidth 360 pt
sidebarWidth 420 pt

The two sidebar widths are the measured numbers in the file. sidebarMinWidth is as narrow as the sidebar goes: each footer row is three equal columns, and a column has to fit its widest reading, a window at 100 %. A number sits in the width of 100% whatever it says, and a reset waits under the pointer in a chip of its own, so no reading is wider than that one. SidebarFooterGeometryTests.theWidestColumnFitsTheMinimumSidebarWidth holds that honest. It was 395 while each vendor row also carried its ctx segment; that moved to the footer's task row, which carries nothing else, so the minimum came back to 360. The context row's widest case — a full window — fits too, held by SidebarFooterGeometryTests.theWidestContextRowFitsTheMinimumSidebarWidth. sidebarWidth is where the sidebar opens with no saved frame, sized to a task row instead: at 360 a row with a Jira key, a diff and a +n squeezes its branch to feat/f…t-side; at 420 the branch keeps its type, the ticket's prefix and its tail.

Some names above share a number — chip/vendorMark at 16, trailingGlyph/chevron at 10, control/projectRow at 28. That is allowed: Metrics has no distinctness rule, only Palette does. Each name answers to a different scale and may move without the other. statusMark is different: it is declared as an alias of trailingGlyph, so the two cannot part.

Typography

The macOS system text scale. AiTerm draws with .system(size:) rather than a text style, so each member is labelled below with the system style it is the size of. A TypeStyle keeps its size, weight and design as separate parts, and its nsFont consults all three — so the handful of AppKit views that take an NSFont can never quietly narrow a style to just its size. A style's .tabular variant sets tabular figures (.monospacedDigit()) in the same face, so a count, a time or a percentage keeps its width as it changes: the system face is for words and numbers, the monospaced face for code alone. Specimens are set at their real size, weight and design.

The four monospaced styles are code: mono a branch name, a shell job's command, a tool call and its JSON, a check's failure output; monoCode a branch in a picker or its field, a completion's name; promptMono the first-prompt editor, which has to match PromptEditor's real NSTextView font exactly, or its placeholder sits where typed text will not; monoChip the terminal-background swatch's #17, a colour's hex digits. Ticket keys, counts, times, telemetry and keycaps are words in the system face.

Sheet

The sheet footprints. Everything inside them measures in Space, Radius and Size.

width 560 pt
Every sheet, including Signals and Settings.
height 560 pt
The sheets whose content runs past any one height and scrolls: New Signal and the Archive; and the most a sheet that fits its content grows to, a NameSheet (New terminal, Add divider, Rename) and Backpack Mode.
creationHeight 500 pt
New Task's and New Review's every step, so the sheet does not jump from one to the next: their prompt editor and ticket checkbox fit under the title and above the footer, and the last step shows the agent fields and the destination summary. A notice in the footer is taller and scrolls the step instead.
queryEditorHeight 56 pt
A signal trigger’s Describe it and query editors; the prompt editor keeps 150 pt.
settingsHeight 580 pt
Settings, whose forms want a slightly taller viewport.
fittingHeight(_:)
Clamps a preferred height to the screen: its visible height less 100 pt, never below 320 pt. A sheet is either .fixed at one of the heights above or .fitting(upTo:), as tall as its content up to one of them (SheetHeight).

Opacity

One fade, for a control that can't be used now. A colour is never faded by hand: that stays Palette's.

disabled 0.4
A segment SegmentedControl's or a tab TabBar's isSelectable rejects, a disabled push button (PushButtonStyle) and a disabled Select, Settings › Operator's Oracle Agent/Model/Reasoning fields while off. Keep role/help text readable and retained choices visible.

Motion

One shared ease-out, so things that settle into place move alike.

settle 0.2 s
Animation.easeOut(duration: 0.2): a toast arriving (SidebarToast). It does not run under Reduce Motion or in a still snapshot.

One theme

AiTerm is dark-only. There is no light variant to keep in sync, and this page commits to the same single theme rather than inventing one the app does not have. Kerning and shadow geometry — blur radius, offset, opacity — are deliberately not tokenised: they are one-off optical corrections on a single element, not a scale anything else draws from. Their absence from Metrics is a decision, not an oversight.

States are a matrix

A component's states are declared up front, not discovered: default, hover, pressed, disabled, focused, selected. A new primitive owes that matrix the same way it owes a name — every variant crossed with every state, decided before the first call site, rather than a hover wash bolted on the week someone notices it is missing.

One rule overrides the matrix: when a target does not exist, the control is absent, not disabled. SidebarView draws no VS Code badge when VS Code is not installed, rather than a greyed one — the branch after it stays on the row as plain text. A disabled control is a promise that the action exists and is currently unavailable — if it can never become available, showing it is a lie the user has to test by clicking.

Reduce Motion is honoured rather than ignored: StatusMark keeps its arc and drops the rotation.

Primitives

Fifteen components, all in app/Sources/AiTermUI/: the fourteen below, and FrontToBackStack, a layout stack that draws nothing of its own and so has no card. They take standard names and no AiTerm type appears in their signature — a primitive that knows what a task is has stopped being a primitive. Each one reads its ground from Surface rather than taking a selected flag.

Every variant below is drawn in HTML at the real numbers from Metrics. Where macOS draws something this page cannot, an SF Symbol or a native menu, the card says so instead of pretending.

Badge

AiTermUI/Badge.swift

The one chip. 16 pt tall (Size.chip) at Radius.chip, labelled in Typography.chip.tabular, words in the system face with tabular figures, on a neutral wash from the surface it sits on. It replaced three bespoke chips — an editor badge, a Jira chip and BranchLabelView's +n chip — that each redrew the same shape. Passing an action makes it a button; without one it draws its shape only. An optional iconTint inks the icon off the accent — a Settings check's green checkmark or amber warning — and yields to white on it like everything else. An optional diff (Badge.Diff(added:removed:)) extends it with signed line counts after its icon and label — +12 −3, green and red, Space.hairline apart, a true minus sign — and leaves out a side that is zero; an empty diff draws nothing extra. An optional suffix (Badge.Suffix(icon:text:)) closes the badge with an icon and a short text, Space.hairline apart and both in the label's ink — a merge request's resolved review threads, a bubble and 2/5; a badge that is only an icon and a suffix is drawn with both. A badge is a chip at its own width, never squeezed or stretched by the row around it. style: .quiet drops the box at rest: no outer padding, the label in the surface's secondaryInk, and the hovered wash drawn Space.tight outside the content so nothing moves; its content shape keeps the gaps between mark and diff clickable. The sidebar's project headers and task and terminal rows use it; everywhere else a badge stays .boxed. markInk: .label inks the mark with the words, the sidebar's badge line, where a row of brand colours competed with the status marks, until Settings › Interface › Sidebar badges turns Brand colours on (BadgeDetails.markInk); the default .own keeps the vendor's colour on a sheet card and in a picker. On a selected row the wash strengthens to badgeSelected and a boxed label lifts to white, while the marks and the diff keep their colours; only on the accent does everything turn white. Passing menu in place of action makes it open a menu — a project header's +n of Jira projects — the same chip with the same hover, and accessibilityLabel says what a bare count cannot. Every token it reads goes through scale.

Use it forA ticket key, a vendor mark, an overflow count, a Settings check, a vendor mark with the diff it opens onto — anything chip-shaped that carries one fact. A new kind of chip is a new content case here, not a new type. .quiet where several sit in one line of text, as on a sidebar row, spaced Space.gap apart.

Icon

AiTermUI/IconSource.swift

Draws an IconSource at a size, optionally overriding its ink. IconSource is the one way to name any mark AiTerm draws — .symbol(String) for an SF Symbol, .brand(Brand) for a single-colour vendor mark, or .artwork(svg:fallback:) for a full-colour SVG that carries its own fallback (.gitlabTanuki, .piBadge) — so a component showing an icon does not care which kind it is. A brand or an artwork fills a size square; a symbol keeps its glyph's own width at that point size. A brand keeps its vendor colour unless tint overrides it: on the accent, where a brand colour reads as a mistake, and on the sidebar's badge line, which inks its marks with its words. A selected row is neutral, so a brand keeps its colour there. A symbol with no tint takes the ink of the surface it sits on; an artwork has no one colour, so a tint reaches only its fallback. The vendor paths live in Logos and are drawn by LogoGlyph, both internal to the module: the one way the app draws a logo, and no fill travels as a hex string.

.symbol("checkmark.circle.fill") SF Symbol · drawn by macOS
.brand(Palette.claude) · 16 pt
.brand(Palette.gitlab) · 18 pt
tint override · on the accent
Use it forAny mark drawn at a Size step. Adding a vendor is one Brand, usable everywhere an IconSource is accepted.
Not forA mark that needs its own shape around it — a filled disc. That is VendorMark or IntegrationMark, both patterns.

FormField

AiTermUI/FormField.swift

A label above its control, at the system's spacing: Typography.label in Palette.muted, then Space.snug, then whatever the caller puts in the builder. It is the only thing in the system that decides how far a label sits from its field. It is a FrontToBackStack, a VStack whose earlier children draw over its later ones, so what its control hangs out of itself (a picker's results, the completion popup) draws over the lines after it with no zIndex; a sheet's fields and steps go in another.

AiTermUI/FormField.swift

Input

AiTermUI/Input.swift

A plain text field in the house field chrome: 28 pt tall (Size.control), Radius.control, filled with Palette.field, a step darker than the ground it sits on, inside a one-point Palette.borderStrong, with Space.inset of horizontal padding. Its binding is proxied so only real edits reach the caller — AppKit hands a field's value back when editing begins and ends, not only when the text changes, so an unproxied setter with a side effect would fire because the user clicked some other field.

Select

AiTermUI/Select.swift

A real NSPopUpButton at .controlSize(.large), which is exactly Size.control, drawn borderless inside the same fieldBox as an Input, so a select and a field side by side are one shape. AppKit still owns the menu, the keyboard and the click; the house draws the chrome, the picked title, Space.inset in, in Typography.body (or monoCode) and Palette.text, and chevron.up.chevron.down in Typography.micro and Palette.muted, centred in a Size.menuRow slot at the trailing edge. Its menu is a window of its own, so it opens over what is below it instead of pushing the sheet around, and it fills the column it is given, which neither SwiftUI's menu-style Picker nor Menu will do: both hug their widest title and centre themselves in what is left. Each value may carry a detail string, which becomes that menu item's tooltip. An optional isSelectable predicate disables individual items while keeping them visible in the native menu. All values are selectable by default; changing the predicate updates existing items, and disabled choices never write the binding. Disabling the whole control still prevents opening its menu.

There is no native bezel: the chrome, the title and the chevrons above are the house's, as the Swift draws them. The chevron is an SF Symbol, drawn here as an approximation. A disabled Select does not dim on its own; whoever disables it fades it with Opacity.disabled. With no width offered, it is as wide as Space.inset, its widest title and the chevron slot.

SegmentedControl

AiTermUI/SegmentedControl.swift

A hand-built segmented control that can carry a logo. 28 pt overall (Size.control, so it lines up with the fields beside it), which is a 24 pt segment inside a 2 pt track, a Radius.control segment inside the track's Radius.group. The track is a field: Palette.field edged in Palette.borderStrong. It is hand-built rather than a Picker because the system control cannot carry a logo and paints its selection in the accent colour. It has one look: Palette.controlActive, the lightest ground, under the selected segment, its label in the surface's ink and the rest in its secondary ink, and the house focus ring, not SwiftUI's compositor halo, around the track while it has the keyboard. It answers to ← and → and skips a segment isSelectable rejects. Tabs are not segments: a sheet's tabs are a TabBar.

Not forA long list, or anything that needs to scroll: that is Select. Nor a sheet's navigation: Settings' panes are a TabBar.

TabBar

AiTermUI/TabBar.swift

A row of underline tabs: Settings' panes. It sits at the foot of a sheet's header, so its selected tab's underline lies on the header's rule. Each tab is its label in Typography.bodyEmphasis, Space.base over its underline, the tabs Space.section apart from the leading edge. No accent: the selection is the label's ink and the bar under it, a Size.tabIndicator bar in Palette.text as wide as the label. The bar is one focusable control: ← and → move the selection among selectable tabs, stopping at the ends. The command-number keys are the sheet's, on hidden buttons (TabShortcuts).

Kbd

AiTermUI/Kbd.swift

Keycaps for a shortcut. Each cap is Size.chip tall with a Size.chip minimum width, at Radius.chip, in Typography.help: keycaps are glyphs, not code, so the system face. A 3 pt gap, narrower than Space.tight, because the caps read as one shortcut rather than two controls side by side. It takes no style: the caps read the Surface they sit on. On .accent, which PushButtonStyle's primary declares, they restate a key equivalent in Palette.onAccent on keycapFill and keycapStroke, white at 22 % and 16 %, which only hold against the accent. Anywhere else they take the surface's ink on its badge wash, edged in Palette.border, as the keyboard section of Settings › Interface lists them.

on Surface.accent · a primary sheet action Create Task ⌘↩
on Surface.accent · Settings Save ⌘↩
on Surface.sheet · a keyboard shortcuts row Remove the task, review or terminal ⌘⌫
Use it forA key equivalent restated on a primary button, or a key listed on a surface; the ground picks the inks. Pass the glyphs macOS menus use — ⌘, ↩ (U+21A9, not U+23CE, which reads heavier at this size), ⎋, ⇧, ⌫. It is hidden from accessibility: read out, it would turn every press into "Create Task command return".
Not forThe secondary button: caps on it read as a second control. And not as a control: it restates a shortcut, it does not handle one.

PushButtonStyle

AiTermUI/PushButtonStyle.swift

The house push button, one shape with a field: Size.control tall, Radius.control, Space.gap either side of its label. Two kinds, used as .buttonStyle(.push(.primary)) and .push(.secondary). .primary, the sheet's one action on ⌘↩, is the accent, its label in Typography.bodyEmphasis and Palette.onAccent, and it declares .surface(.accent) so its keycaps and a busy mark ink for it. .secondary, everything else (Cancel, Back, a card's action), is Palette.button, lighter than the ground it stands on, inside a one-point Palette.border, its label in Typography.body and Palette.text. It is a ButtonStyle, so the button stays a native Button: .keyboardShortcut, .disabled, .help and its accessibility work as they do on AppKit's bezel. In the scaled sidebar it scales its own height, radius and padding.

SearchField

AiTermUI/SearchField.swift

A single-line field whose AppKit delegate gives an open popup first refusal on navigation commands — SwiftUI's TextField exposes no such hook, which is the whole reason this is an NSViewRepresentable rather than an Input. It wears the same house chrome as Input (Size.control, Radius.control, Palette.field inside Palette.borderStrong) and sets its text in Typography.body. Focus may be requested before SwiftUI has inserted it into a window, so it retries at window attachment rather than dropping the request.

SidebarHeading

AiTermUI/SidebarHeading.swift

A heading in the sidebar's own voice: the section face (Typography.section, 11 semibold) in the third ink (Palette.tertiary), its words as given. Sentence case, never uppercased and never tracked: the caller's string is what is drawn, so a divider keeps its name as the person typed it. Drawn in the sidebar, it scales through its one token, which scales by itself. Its face and ink are public (SidebarHeading.style, .ink) for the one heading that draws its own words, the Operator's while it decodes. It has no states: it is a label, never a control.

Hairline

AiTermUI/Hairline.swift

The one 1 pt rule. By default the soft Palette.border, the same stroke as a card's edge; .firm draws the firm Palette.borderStrong a field is outlined in, for a short rule that has to hold on its own: the connectors between a sheet's steps. A rectangle rather than SwiftUI's Divider, so it stays horizontal inside an HStack, where Divider turns vertical. The sheets used to lay a Divider under the border, which read a third brighter; that second weight was folded into this one. A stroke, so it does not scale.

Patterns

These are AiTerm compositions, not library parts. They live in app/Sources/AiTerm/Views/, keep AiTerm names, carry AiTerm concepts, and are built only from the primitives above. A pattern is promoted to a primitive only when two or more files use it and it carries no AiTerm type and it is not app-shell composition — a sheet's own anatomy, a window's chrome — which stays here regardless of reuse. Sidebar footer

SidebarFooter: System, then Usage, split by a rule, on Palette.sidebarFooter. Every row is its mark at Size.vendorMark, Space.inset, then three columns of equal width Space.gap apart, each one reading built the same way: its label in Palette.muted, Space.tight, a UsageRing at Size.statusMark, a space, its number in Palette.text (amber past the threshold), all in Typography.help.tabular on a Size.menuRow line. The label sits in the width of the widest label and the number in the width of 100%, so the rings stand in three straight lines down the footer whatever the digits.

A vendor's weekly window is its first column, being the one every vendor has: Codex reports nothing else, so a missing reading is always a later column, as on the context's row. The Mac's row is cpu, ram and bat, the battery only while it is the Mac's power; while Backpack Mode is on or switching, a second row holds the mode's line across the row, a ToneRing at Size.statusMarkSmall, Space.tight, then its words, both in the mode's SettingsTone. A vendor's note spans the row. When a window clears is shown under the pointer only: a ResetBadge, resets Sat 12:00, on a Size.chip chip of Palette.menu inside Palette.borderStrong, just above the reading. At rest the row is the numbers alone.

Background work

Supporting projections and coordinators stay beside their owning pattern. The Swift type inventory and AiTermUI/README.md define reuse boundaries.

Signals and the Operator

SignalOperatorRow opens the active workload’s chat; a signal's heading is a HeadingRow, drawn from its HeadingValue on the project heading's grid: source mark, fold and counts. The Operator's heading is a SectionHeading: its + menu holds New Signal… alone, and Pause Operator / Resume Operator sit in its context menu. TaskRowView uses the same two-line title and badge grid under a project or signal, with no extra Operator line. When work finishes the chat closes and its row disappears, while signals keep polling. The next matching workload starts a fresh chat. These are native Swift renders of synthetic fixtures at the standard scale, captured on 16 Nov 2026. Values remain defined by Palette and Metrics.

Only the Operator’s activity caption decodes. OperatorBadge uses DecodeWordsView for 0.5 seconds per event, including consecutive events with identical words. The title stays “Operator”. Each start, result, failure and return to watching gets a new runtime identity; new activity replaces the previous action immediately. OperatorActivityCaption holds quick completed actions for one second (decode plus reading time), so an event that finishes within a display frame remains visible. Status marks remain current. The words retain their ink, case and width. Reduce Motion swaps; snapshots stand still. Context renewal waits for a safe boundary at 150,000 tokens; age alone does not restart the chat.

StateDrawn behavior
Launching / working / watchingOne status mark and the ordinary 52 pt, two-line task row. Task badges stay visible and never decode. A watching task does not poll its transcript.
Question / permission / blockedAmber means the person acts. Questions open the Operator chat; a worker permission opens its own window. Own permission prompts outrank acts.
Paused / switched offUnfinished work retains its paused row. Without work, “Operator · paused” remains in the heading; its context menu offers Resume Operator. Workers finish their turn and wait. Switch On previews never-started matches.
Folded / removed sourceFolded status counts share the project recipe. Removed-source help explains existing tasks carry on with saved instructions.
No unfinished workEnabled, unpaused signals poll without a chat row. A global pause is visible in the Operator heading and its context menu always offers Resume Operator. A kept completed task remains without keeping the chat open. A real global question or close failure remains actionable.
Done / Take Over / closed windowDone uses ordinary task vocabulary. Take Over moves the row to its project. A closed window resumes its conversation on click.

One family of creation sheets

SteppedSheet with its Steps, SheetStepper, SteppedSheetFooter and CreationClosingBlock share chrome, completed-step navigation and the effect of the current picks. Task and Review use three steps: Task or Review (where it comes from and where it lives, on one page), Prompt, Agent. SignalSheet uses five: Signal, Starts when, Prompt, Agents, Done when. Every step's footer has Cancel at the leading end, then Back from step 2 and the primary at the trailing end: Continue, or the create label on the last step. A failure is a Notice over that row (CreationNotices), and its fix, when it has one, sits under the notice (CreationRecoveryButton). ProjectSheet combines folder, Jira links and worktree import; NameSheet handles Terminal and Divider. Inapplicable steps are omitted, never reordered.

Labels sit above their controls in Typography.label, Space.snug apart; help uses Typography.help; fields use Space.block. Optional labels end “(optional)”. SegmentedControl asks two/three short alternatives; Select chooses a growing list; native checkboxes ask independent booleans; Input asks one line; PromptEditor asks prose, descriptions and queries; a FormField may carry a small push button (.controlSize(.small)) at the trailing end of its label row; ChipsPicker searches items. Agent, Model and Reasoning are one select row, a list for a signal.

OperatorSettingsPane and OracleGroup

Three groups: Operator, Oracle and Steer the Operator. Role bullets and help explain what each does, never does and how to steer it. The Operator chooses Model/Reasoning; the Oracle chooses Agent/Model/Reasoning in one row. Off keeps the Oracle choices and fades only those fields to Opacity.disabled. Instructions use PromptEditor. Save applies current standing instructions to the chat and Oracle checks.

SignalQuestionNotification opens the active Operator row/window; the ordinary worker permission notification opens the worker. Resolved questions withdraw their notifications.

Notice

Every “needs your attention or your answer” in the app is one Notice: an amber exclamationmark.circle.fill at Size.inlineMark, Space.snug before the title in Typography.label and Palette.text on one row; the description under it in Typography.help and Palette.muted; then any extra content; then the actions as links Space.gap apart; Space.tight between the rows and nothing indented. No amber text: the mark carries the tone. It is the sidebar banner's failed operation (IssueBanner) and failed save, iTerm2 refusing the connection (SidebarConnectionBanner), a failed create in New Task's or New Review's footer (CreationNotices), New Signal's error and readiness, and the Backpack Mode sheet's permission ask. In a sheet's footer the Notice has no links: the footer's buttons are its actions, a failure with one sentence is the title alone, and a failure's fix sits under it as a secondary push button with no key (CreationRecoveryButton), ⌘↩ staying the create. Not Notices: the grey line while iTerm2 connects (a HelpText), field help, row captions, toasts; on the sidebar a question is the Operator row's needs-you badge.

How this tab works

Proposals

Nothing on this tab is in the code yet. A proposal is a change drawn at real size from the current tokens, with its options side by side, so it can be chosen before any Swift is written. Foundations and Components describe what ships; this tab describes what might.

Once a proposal is picked and implemented, it is deleted from here and the other two tabs are synced to the Swift. The tab itself stays, even when it has nothing on it.

No open proposals.
